papers.name: Paper 1
papers.covers: Key concepts in biology; Cells and control; Genetics; Natural selection and genetic modification; Health, disease and the development of medicines. The core practicals for those topics. Worth 50% of the GCSE. Higher tier, grades 4 to 9. At least 10% of the marks assess maths skills, and a formulae sheet is not provided: the few equations (magnification, rates, percentage change) are recalled. The paper is ten questions, all compulsory, mixing multiple choice, short answer, calculations and extended open response. 27 of the 100 marks are overlap questions that also appear on the Foundation paper.

papers.name: Paper 2
papers.covers: Key concepts in biology again; Plant structures and their functions; Animal coordination, control and homeostasis; Exchange and transport in animals; Ecosystems and material cycles. The core practicals for those topics. Worth 50% of the GCSE. Higher tier, grades 4 to 9. Questions may draw on Paper 1 knowledge. The paper is ten questions, all compulsory, mixing multiple choice, short answer, calculations and extended open response. 27 of the 100 marks are overlap questions that also appear on the Foundation paper. At least 10% of the marks across the two papers assess maths skills, and a formulae sheet is not provided.

commandWords.meaning: One-mark recall. A word, a number, or a short phrase; no explanation wanted.
Say what happens or what something is like, in order. No reasons needed. For a graph: the shape, with numbers from it.
Give reasons. Every point should have a "because" or a "so". The number of marks tells you how many linked points.
Show the working, give the answer, give the unit. Rate questions need a time in the denominator.
Say how two things are similar or how they differ. Your answer has to mention both things, in the same sentence where you can: "A has more X than B". No conclusion is needed.
Use the information and your knowledge to weigh both sides, then give a judgement that follows from what you said.
Plan or invent a procedure from existing ideas: say what you change, what you keep the same, what you measure and how, and how many repeats.
Draw a conclusion from the information given, showing the step from evidence to conclusion.
Use given data or a graph to find a value, usually with a calculation or a reading you show.
Give the evidence or reasoning that supports the statement, usually from the data in the question.
Apply your knowledge to a new situation. There may be more than one acceptable answer; a sensible reason earns the mark.
Say what result you expect, using the pattern in the data or the biology. A reason is only needed if the question also says explain.
Set out the issue, then explore it from more than one angle by reasoning or argument. Often a longer, level-marked answer, so structure and scientific vocabulary matter.

Draw with a sharp pencil, using a ruler where the shape calls for straight lines; freehand is allowed. Plot points as small crosses, choose a sensible scale, label axes with units, and draw a line of best fit, not dot-to-dot.
Say what the data shows and whether it supports the claim, with a number from the data.
Give at least one similarity and at least one difference. Both things must appear in the answer; no conclusion is needed.
Weigh up all the relevant factors, say which matter most, and come to a conclusion where one is asked for.
Pick out the key information from the data, diagram or passage you have been given. No explanation wanted.
Give the meaning of the term. There is usually more than one acceptable wording.
Finish the table or diagram you are given by adding the missing entries.
Make the point, then link ideas to justify it. Both halves are marked.
A statement has already been made; you only have to say why it is so.
Find an approximate value from a diagram, from given data, or by a rough calculation.

assessmentObjectives.meaning: Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of ideas, techniques, and procedures.
Apply knowledge and understanding: unfamiliar organisms, data, calculations, practical contexts.
Analyse information to interpret, evaluate, draw conclusions, and improve experimental procedures.

grade9ByQuestionType.questionType: Explain a process or adaptation (AO1/AO2, 2 to 4 marks)
grade9ByQuestionType.looksLike: Names the structure, states the feature, and links it to the function with a "so that": a root hair cell has a large surface area so that more water can be absorbed by osmosis. Each mark is a linked pair, not a list of words.

grade9ByQuestionType.questionType: Data and graph analysis (AO3, 3 to 4 marks)
grade9ByQuestionType.looksLike: Quotes numbers from the graph with units, describes the trend including where it levels off, and explains the biology behind the shape, such as which factor is limiting on each part of the curve.

grade9ByQuestionType.questionType: Core practical method or evaluation (AO3, 4 to 6 marks)
grade9ByQuestionType.looksLike: Names the independent, dependent, and control variables, says how each is measured or kept constant, gives repeats and a mean, and spots the specific weakness in a given method rather than a generic one.
Sets out the equation, converts units first, gives the answer to a sensible number of significant figures with the unit, such as mm per minute or bubbles per minute.
A planned answer with a clear line of argument, the correct vocabulary throughout, both sides where a judgement is asked for, and a conclusion that follows from the points made.
